node-1.label: A patient in their 50s presented with recurrent abdominal pain and syncope after drinking alcohol, with symptoms worsening on admission

node-2.label: Symptoms usually occurred 6-20 hours after alcohol ingestion and lasted 5-10 minutes; syncope occurred only after large alcohol intake

node-3.label: Past medical history included hypertension diagnosed 3 months prior; social history included smoking and alcohol overconsumption (250g/week) for about 20 years

node-4.label: No specific physical examination findings were documented in the case report

why.why: Both laboratory and radiology experts support alcohol-related cardiovascular syncope, citing the ECG pattern of high-degree AV block, ventricular tachycardia, and widespread ST-segment elevation with only mild coronary stenosis and normal troponin, plus the 6–20 hour post-drinking onset. However, the new limitations they raise—echocardiography and continuous telemetry were not obtained, and blood alcohol level was never confirmed—leave structural heart disease and arrhythmia burden unverified, tempering confidence from 0.85 to 0.80.

The laboratory expert explicitly excludes an alcoholic GI emergency based on normal biochemistry and lack of abdominal findings, and the radiology expert also favors a cardiovascular cause. No new supporting evidence emerged, so confidence is reduced from 0.08 to 0.05.

The laboratory expert excludes alcoholic metabolic disorder because routine biochemistry is normal, while the ECG provides a direct cardiac explanation. This new explicit expert exclusion reduces confidence from 0.07 to 0.05.
